turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Good morning, everyone-thanks for joining our Q3 all-hands on Zoom. I’m thrilled to kick things off with the headline numbers that really tell the story of where we are and where we’re heading.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sounds great, Nadia.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alright, let’s dive in. Our annual recurring revenue is now $8.4 million, up from $6.1 million at the end of Q2, which translates to a 38 percent year-over-year growth rate.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Impressive.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Even more encouraging is our net revenue retention, which sits at 118 percent-meaning existing customers are not just staying, they’re expanding their contracts at a healthy pace.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: That’s solid.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’ve also grown our headcount to 62 employees across product, engineering, sales, and support, up from 55 last quarter, and we’re still operating with a runway of roughly 26 months at our current burn rate.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Nice work.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: A quick snapshot of the top-line: we closed 14 new logos this quarter, with an average contract value of $210 k, and we added $2.3 million in new ARR from our enterprise pipeline.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Cool.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Geographically, North America contributed 57 percent of the new ARR, EMEA 29 percent, and APAC the remaining 14 percent. Those numbers reflect the success of our localized go-to-market strategies and the strong product-market fit we’ve been iterating on.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That’s a big win for the sales team.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly, Alex. And on the product side, the latest release of Cadence Query Engine 3.2 rolled out to all customers without any major regressions, which helped us maintain that high NRR figure.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: And the finance side?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: From a financial perspective, our operating expense grew to $4.9 million this quarter, largely driven by the new hires in engineering and the expanded sales org, but the increase is fully offset by the ARR growth, keeping our EBITDA margin in line with our target range of 12-15 percent.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Good to hear.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Finally, a quick note on cash: with $12.4 million in cash on hand, the 26-month runway gives us ample runway to execute the strategic initiatives we’ll outline later, including the upcoming VPC-ready enterprise tier and the next major scalability upgrade.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Looking forward to that.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: So, to sum up: $8.4 M ARR, 118% NRR, 62 teammates, 26-month runway, and a clear path forward. That’s the high-level picture, and now let’s break down where the growth came from and which segment underperformed.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alright, let’s dig into the sources of that growth - the first thing to note is that our enterprise segment delivered the lion’s share, pulling in $5.1 million of the $8.4 million ARR, which is a 42 percent jump from Q2.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That’s the result of the two big deals we closed in July and September - the Global Retail Corp contract at $1.9 million and the FinTech Solutions partnership at $2.3 million, both multi-year and with built-in upsell clauses.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly, and those wins were powered by the new Cadence Query Engine 3.2 features - the federated search and real-time analytics that our prospects kept asking for.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a finance lens, the enterprise lift also helped us improve the average contract value from $180 k last quarter to $210 k this quarter, which is a nice bump.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: On the mid-market side we added $2.0 million in ARR, driven largely by the expansion of our existing customer base - we saw a 15 percent upsell rate in Q3, which is higher than the 9 percent we hit in Q2.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And the churn in that segment stayed low, right?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Right, churn was only 2.3 percent overall, and in mid-market it was 1.8 percent, so the net revenue retention stayed solid at 118 percent.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: What about the small-business tier?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: That’s where we hit a snag. Our SMB segment only contributed $1.2 million this quarter, down from $1.7 million in Q2 - a 29 percent decline.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Any particular reason for the dip?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Two main factors: first, the pricing refresh we rolled out in May unintentionally narrowed the sweet spot for companies under $500 k ARR, and second, the August outage - that four-hour blackout - hit a handful of our SMB customers who rely on the platform for daily reporting, causing some to defer renewals.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: We also saw that the inbound lead volume from the SMB channel fell about 12 percent, probably because our recent webinars were more enterprise-focused.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’ve already started a remediation plan - a targeted discount program for the affected SMB accounts and a revamped webinar series aimed at the $250 k-$500 k ARR bracket, which should help us claw back the lost momentum in Q4.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: And the financial impact of that underperformance is roughly $300 k in missed ARR, which we’ve already accounted for in our revised forecast.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: So to recap: enterprise drove $5.1 million, mid-market added $2.0 million, SMB slipped to $1.2 million - that’s the growth story and the one segment we need to refocus on moving forward.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Alright, let me walk through the numbers on burn and runway, and then touch on the board conversation we had last week.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: First, our quarterly cash burn came in at $4.2 million, which is actually $200k lower than we projected in the Q2 budget.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: The main driver for that reduction was the delayed hiring in the data science team-those headcount approvals were pushed back by a month, saving us roughly $120k in salary expense.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: On the expense side, we also trimmed the third-party vendor spend on the new marketing analytics stack by about $80k after renegotiating the contract.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: If you look at the burn rate month-over-month, we went from $1.45M in July, down to $1.35M in August, and $1.4M in September, averaging about $1.38M per month for Q3.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Given our current cash balance of $7.8 million, that puts us at a runway of roughly 26 months at the current burn, which is comfortably above the 18-month threshold we set for strategic flexibility.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Now, about the board meeting-there were three key points they focused on: the ARR growth to $8.4M, the net revenue retention holding at 118%, and the cash runway we just discussed.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: The CFO’s office presented a sensitivity analysis showing that even if we see a 10% dip in SMB ARR next quarter, we still have over 20 months of runway, which the board found reassuring.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: They also asked hard questions about the August outage cost; I broke that down to $45k in immediate remediation and an estimated $120k in potential churn, which we’re already offsetting with the discount program Nadia mentioned.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: One thing that came up was the upcoming Series B extension-we’re planning to raise an additional $15 million at a $150 million pre-money valuation, and the board signaled they’re supportive as long as we keep the burn under $5M quarterly.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: They liked the fact that we have a clear path to profitability by Q2 2025, driven by the enterprise lift and the higher average contract value you all highlighted earlier.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: In terms of capital allocation, the board approved an extra $500k for the query engine rewrite that Daniel is leading, because they see that as a strategic moat.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Overall, the tone was positive-they’re comfortable with the current cash position, see the runway as healthy, and appreciate the disciplined approach we’ve taken to manage burn while still delivering growth.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: So to sum up, burn is down, runway is 26 months, and the board left the meeting with confidence that we’re on track to hit the next milestones without needing a drastic financing round right now.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Okay, let me dive into the pipeline because that’s where the momentum really shows up this quarter.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: We closed $2.1 million in new ARR in Q3, which is roughly 25% of the $8.4 million total ARR we just announced.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: But the real story is the enterprise side - we have two big deals that are now in the final contract stage.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: First, the deal with GlobalFin, a $3.2 million three-year agreement that will roll out across their North America and EMEA operations starting January.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: We’ve already completed a proof-of-concept in their London data center, and the engineering team showed them how our new VPC-isolated deployment can meet their compliance requirements without any extra licensing.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: The second one is with HealthSync, a $2.7 million contract for a multi-tenant SaaS solution that includes custom analytics dashboards and a dedicated support tier.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: HealthSync’s CTO was impressed by the query engine rewrite that Daniel just got green-lit - they see it as the key to scaling their reporting workloads tenfold.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Both deals are slated to close by the end of next month, which means we’ll be adding roughly $5.9 million of ARR in Q4, pushing our annualized run rate past $14 million if we hit both.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: In terms of the broader pipeline, we have about $12 million in qualified opportunities, with $4.5 million in the $1M-plus bucket.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Our SMB segment is still the engine - we added $1.4 million of ARR from 45 new logos, most of them through the self-serve channel that Nadia highlighted earlier.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I’m also hearing from the sales ops team that the average sales cycle for enterprise is now 5.2 months, down from 6.1 months last quarter, thanks to the faster demo environment we rolled out in July.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: That’s a direct result of the product-led onboarding flow we built with Sarah’s help - the time from demo request to PoC sign-off dropped from 21 days to 14 days.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: One caveat - we still have a handful of deals stuck in legal because of the new data residency clauses the board asked us to add after the August outage.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: We’re working with the legal team to streamline that, and I expect we’ll clear the backlog by early November.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: So, to sum up, the pipeline is healthy, the two enterprise wins are on the brink, and we’re on track to exceed $14 million ARR by year-end if everything stays on schedule.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Alright, let me jump in on the query engine rewrite - this is the biggest under-the-hood change we’ve done since the platform launch back in Q1.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: First off, the old engine was built on a monolithic Node.js stack that basically did a full table scan for any report over a million rows, which, as you can imagine, was choking us during the HealthSync PoC.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: We’ve now moved to a hybrid architecture: the front-end query parser stays in TypeScript, but the heavy lifting is delegated to a Rust-based execution engine that runs in a separate microservice.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: What that means in plain English is sub-second latency for most of the ad-hoc dashboards that used to take 30-45 seconds to render.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: We benchmarked it against the old system on a 10 GB dataset - the average query time dropped from 32 seconds to 0.9 seconds, and the 99th percentile went from 78 seconds down to 2.3 seconds.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: The rewrite also introduced columnar storage for the fact tables, which slashes I/O by about 70% and lets us keep more data in memory.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: From a developer standpoint, the new engine exposes a gRPC API, so we can spin up language-agnostic clients - Python, Go, even Java - without pulling in the whole Node stack.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: That’s why HealthSync’s CTO was so excited - they have a data science team that writes custom notebooks in Python, and now they can query our engine directly without any ETL lag.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: We also added a built-in query planner that does predicate pushdown and automatic join reordering, which is why the same query that used to hit the database three times now hits it once.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: In terms of operational impact, the new service runs in a separate Kubernetes namespace with its own autoscaling rules - we set a target CPU utilization of 65%, and during peak load in the August outage we saw the pod count scale from 4 to 12 in under a minute.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: The rewrite cost us about $420 k in engineering time over the last two months, but we’re already seeing a ROI: the reduced compute time saves us roughly $15 k per month on our cloud bill, and the faster reporting is a direct upsell lever for enterprise.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Looking ahead, the next step is to expose a GraphQL layer on top of the gRPC API so product teams can compose queries without writing any code - that’s slated for Q1 next year.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: So, to sum up, the rewrite unlocks three things: massive performance gains for end-users, lower infrastructure spend, and a more flexible developer platform that we can monetize in future product tiers.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alright, before we move on to Q4 priorities, I need to address the one thing that went badly this quarter - the four-hour outage we had on August 12th.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Yeah, that was a rough one. We lost revenue for a few key customers.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly. Let me walk through what happened, why it happened, and what we’re doing to make sure it doesn’t happen again.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: At 02:17 UTC we started seeing a spike in CPU utilization on the primary database shard that powers the real-time analytics pipeline. Our monitoring alerts fired, but the auto-scale policy we had in place was mis-configured - the threshold was set to 85% instead of the 70% we normally use.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: And because the shard was on a single-node RDS instance, once it hit that ceiling the queries started queuing, which in turn backed up the entire request chain.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Right, and the queue length hit 12,000 requests within five minutes. Our load balancer kept routing traffic to that node because the health check was still passing - the CPU was high but the process was alive, so the LB thought everything was fine.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: So the health check didn’t catch the overload?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly. The health check only verifies a TCP handshake, not actual query latency. That’s a gap we missed in our observability checklist.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: The financial impact was roughly $45 k in lost billable minutes, plus we had to honor SLAs for three enterprise accounts, which added another $12 k in credits.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We also had a cascade effect: the analytics service that feeds the dashboard UI timed out, causing the front-end to display a generic error page for all users, which is why the outage felt so total.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Did the outage affect the new query engine you just rolled out?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Fortunately, the Rust-based query engine lives in a separate namespace and was insulated - it kept running, but the UI couldn’t fetch the data to render, so users still saw a blank screen.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: In terms of root cause, we identified three primary failures: a mis-configured auto-scale policy, an insufficient health-check metric, and a lack of circuit-breaker logic in the request router.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: We’ve already added a circuit-breaker that will short-circuit traffic to the overloaded shard after latency exceeds 2 seconds, and it will automatically route to a read-replica.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We also rewrote the auto-scale policy to trigger at 70% CPU and added a secondary metric - average query latency - as a guardrail. The new policy was tested in staging with a simulated spike and it scaled from 4 to 10 pods in under 30 seconds.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a financial perspective, the fix should prevent any repeat of the $57 k hit we saw, and the additional redundancy will actually save us about $8 k per month in avoided downtime.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Finally, we’ve instituted a post-mortem review cadence - a 48-hour internal review, a written report, and a cross-functional retro next week. The goal is zero repeat incidents of this class.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Sounds thorough. Thanks for the honesty, Nadia.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Thanks, everyone. Let’s keep the momentum and make sure our systems are as reliable as our growth numbers.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alright, let’s pivot to Q4. We’ve boiled down the next quarter to three concrete priorities that will keep the growth trajectory and shore up the reliability we just talked about.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Sounds good, Nadia. I’m curious how those line up with the pipeline you mentioned earlier.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: First priority: launch the self-serve onboarding flow for SMBs by the end of November. Right now our conversion funnel from trial to paid is 4.2%, and the manual onboarding bottleneck is costing us roughly $150k in missed ARR each month.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: That ties into the backend too - we need the new auth microservice ready to handle the expected 30% increase in concurrent sign-ups.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly, Daniel. The second priority is to finish the multi-region replication for the analytics data store. We saw that outage expose how a single-region failure can knock out dashboards, and with the upcoming enterprise VPC contracts we can’t afford that latency spike again.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a financial lens, the replication will reduce our projected downtime cost by about $22k per quarter, which improves our runway outlook.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Third priority: roll out the new enterprise tier with built-in VPC isolation and custom SLA dashboards. The two big deals Alex flagged - the $2.3M contract with FinEdge and the $1.9M agreement with HealthSync - both require that feature set, and we need it live for Q4-end to meet their go-live dates.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Just to add, the HealthSync timeline is early December, so we’re on a tight schedule, but the engineering effort is already 70% complete.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Right, and to make that happen we’re reallocating two senior engineers from the query-engine polishing sprint to the VPC workstream, which will shave roughly three weeks off the critical path.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Will that impact any front-end deliverables we have scheduled for the next release?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Good question. The front-end team will still ship the new dashboard widgets on the existing timeline - the only trade-off is we’ll push the dark-mode redesign to Q1 next year.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And the customer-success tooling? We’ve got the new health-score model ready, but it needs the analytics replication to feed real-time data.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Sarah, that’s why the replication priority is #2 - it’s the foundation for both the enterprise tier and the health-score dashboards. We expect the replication to be in production by mid-December, giving you a buffer to integrate the model before the year-end reporting cycle.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Just a heads-up - the multi-region rollout will require a brief maintenance window of about two hours on the 14th, but we’ll coordinate with support to notify all affected customers.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: And we’ve already accounted for that downtime in the budget; it’s a $5k expense versus the $45k we lost last quarter from the outage.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: So to recap: self-serve SMB onboarding by Nov 30, multi-region analytics replication by Dec 15, and the enterprise VPC tier live by Dec 31. Hitting these three will lock in at least $3.2M of ARR from the new deals and improve our net revenue retention to stay above 118%.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I’ll sync with sales to make sure the pipeline numbers reflect those dates and keep the reps aligned on the onboarding rollout.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Great. Any blockers we need to surface now?

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Just need clarity on the budget for the extra engineering headcount.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: The CFO approved an additional $120k for contractor support in Q4, specifically earmarked for the VPC workstream, so we’re good there.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: That keeps us on track for the 26-month runway we quoted, even with the modest increase in burn.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Perfect. Let’s all own our pieces, keep the communication tight, and we’ll close Q4 strong.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Hey everyone, quick one - I’ve been hearing a lot of chatter on the team about a possible hiring freeze. Can you confirm whether we’re actually freezing hires right now?

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I think the vibe has been mixed, Rachel. Some of the GTM folks are definitely pausing a few roles, but I’m not sure if it’s a formal freeze across the board.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a finance standpoint, we didn’t get a blanket freeze memo. The board approved the Q4 budget, which includes a modest increase in headcount spend, especially for the VPC workstream.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: I’ve got a couple of open positions on the solutions side that we were hoping to fill before the holidays. If there’s a freeze, that could really slow us down.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Same on the engineering side - we have a junior dev spot that’s been in the pipeline for the query rewrite. If we can’t bring them on, we might push the timeline.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Right, I get that. I just want to make sure we’re not sending mixed signals. People are asking on Slack if they should keep interviewing or put it on hold.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: I hear you, Rachel. Let me be crystal clear: there is no hiring freeze at Cadence.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But I’ve also heard that we’re slowing down hiring in go-to-market. Is that true?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly. We’re being more disciplined - we’re still hiring, but we’re prioritising critical roles that directly impact our Q4 deliverables, like the VPC engineers and the enterprise sales reps.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: So for us in growth, that means we’ll still bring on the two enterprise account execs we’ve been talking about, but we might hold off on the junior SDRs until after Q1.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From the cash-flow side, this approach keeps our burn in line with the runway of 26 months we quoted, while still letting us hit the $3.2 M ARR target from the new deals.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Got it. Just to close the loop - if someone gets an offer in the next two weeks, we should move forward, right?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Yes, any offer that aligns with the priority list - VPC, enterprise sales, key engineering - should be approved. Anything outside that scope can be revisited in Q1.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Thanks, Nadia. That helps a lot. I’ll let the solutions team know we can keep the health-score model hiring on track.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: And I’ll push the extra contractor budget to get the query-engine rewrite done without further delays.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Appreciate the clarity, everyone. I’ll update the channel and make sure the recruiting team knows the go-to-market hiring cadence.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Nadia, just to be crystal clear for everyone watching the recording, are we officially in a hiring freeze across the company?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: No, there is absolutely no hiring freeze at Cadence. We are still adding headcount where it matters.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Got it, thanks. But I’ve also heard some chatter that the go-to-market hiring pace is being throttled. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Yes, that’s correct. We’re being more disciplined in the go-to-market function. We’re still hiring, but we’re prioritising the roles that have a direct impact on our Q4 objectives-namely the VPC engineers, the enterprise sales reps, and a few senior product marketers.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: So for growth, does that mean the two enterprise account executives we discussed stay on track?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly. Those two senior execs are still green-lit because they’re tied to the $3.2 M ARR target we outlined for Q4. The junior SDR pipeline, however, will be put on hold until after the first quarter of next year.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a cash-flow perspective, that slower go-to-market hiring actually helps us keep the burn rate aligned with the 26-month runway we quoted, while still letting us hit the revenue milestones.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: And if an offer comes in for a senior VPC engineer next week, do we move forward?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Yes, any offer that aligns with the priority list-VPC, enterprise sales, key engineering-should be approved immediately. Those hires are essential for the VPC rollout we announced in early August and for delivering the query-engine rewrite that Daniel’s team is working on.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Just to add, the extra contractor budget we secured will let us finish the rewrite without needing a full-time junior dev right now, which buys us a little more flexibility.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: That’s a good point, Daniel. The contractor window gives us the bandwidth to meet the August-September delivery window for the new indexing feature, and it also reduces the risk of over-committing headcount before we see the impact of the VPC deployments on our enterprise pipeline.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: On the solutions side, we have the health-score model team that was planning to bring on a data-science lead in January. Does the slower go-to-market cadence affect that?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: No, the health-score model is classified under product-engineering, not go-to-market, so that hire stays on schedule. We want that capability in place before we launch the next version of our analytics dashboard in Q1.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Okay, so to sum up: no freeze, but a tighter filter on which roles move forward now, focusing on VPC, enterprise sales, and key engineering. Everything else gets delayed until after Q1.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly. And just so everyone knows, we’ll be publishing an updated hiring priority sheet on the internal wiki by end of day tomorrow. It will list the approved roles, the target start dates, and the budget owners. If you have any questions about where a specific role falls, ping me or James directly.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: One quick follow-up-do we have a revised headcount number for Q4 now that we’ve narrowed the scope?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’re looking at roughly 64 new hires for the quarter, down from the 70 we originally projected, because we’re shaving about six junior SDR spots and a couple of non-critical support roles. The net effect is still a net increase of 12 employees over the previous quarter, bringing us to 62 total FTEs at the end of Q4, which matches the runway model we shared last week.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Thanks, Nadia. That really clears things up for the whole team.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Nadia, can you walk us through what the enterprise tier actually looks like now that we’ve got the VPC rollout coming up? I mean, are we bundling the new indexing feature with the VPC, or is that still a separate add-on?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Sure, happy to clarify. The enterprise tier is essentially our full-stack package: we’ve got the core Cadence platform, the advanced analytics suite, plus the VPC isolation layer that we announced on August 3rd, and the new indexing feature that Daniel’s team is delivering in September. All three are packaged together as a single price point for accounts over $500 K ARR.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: Just to add a quick financial spin-because the VPC adds about $15 K per seat in infrastructure cost, we’ve built that cost into the enterprise tier pricing, so the gross margin stays roughly at our target 71% for those accounts.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Got it. And the VPC-does that mean each enterprise customer gets a dedicated virtual private cloud, or are we talking shared tenancy with network policies?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Each enterprise customer gets its own isolated VPC environment. We’re using AWS’s native VPC constructs, so it’s a true logical separation-different subnets, security groups, and routing tables per client. That’s why we needed the extra contractor budget Daniel mentioned, to handle the automation of provisioning and the Terraform modules.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Exactly. The rewrite of the query engine now supports multi-tenant indexing, but the VPC layer adds a per-tenant namespace, which means we can enforce data residency and compliance rules on a per-customer basis without impacting the shared query cache.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: And from a solutions perspective, does that change how we sell the enterprise tier? Like, do we need to do a separate proof-of-concept for VPC isolation?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: We’ve built a demo environment that spins up a mock VPC in under five minutes, so the sales team can walk prospects through the isolation features live. The only extra step is the security-review checklist, which our compliance team has already signed off for the standard VPC configuration.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: Just a quick follow-up-how does this affect our pipeline numbers? Are we expecting the VPC to close more deals, or is it more of a churn-prevention tool?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Both, actually. The VPC is a major differentiator for the two enterprise deals we have in flight-one with FinTechCo, which required strict data-isolation for PCI compliance, and another with HealthData Inc., which needs HIPAA-level segregation. Those deals are each projected at $1.2 M ARR, and the VPC was the clincher. At the same time, we’re seeing lower churn in existing enterprise accounts because they now have the ability to spin up isolated environments for new business units without asking us to build custom solutions.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: That makes sense. Do we have any metrics on how many VPCs we’ve already provisioned for customers this quarter?

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: We rolled out the first production VPC for a beta customer on August 21st, and since then we’ve provisioned seven more for pilot accounts. The automation pipeline can handle up to 20 new VPCs per week, so capacity isn’t a bottleneck.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Great. One last thing-if a customer wants a custom VPC configuration, like a specific CIDR block or additional NAT gateways, are we able to accommodate that within the enterprise tier, or does that become a professional services engagement?

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Standard customizations-like choosing a CIDR block from our approved ranges or adding extra NAT gateways-are covered under the enterprise tier. Anything beyond that, such as dedicated hardware or cross-region VPC peering, would be a separate professional services scope, and we’d bill it as an add-on. Our sales playbook now includes a quick decision tree to flag those cases early.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Perfect, that clears up a lot. Thanks, everyone.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Alright, I think we’ve covered all the major updates, so I want to take a minute to wrap things up and give a shout-out to a couple of folks who really went above and beyond this quarter.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: First, Rachel, your work on the new onboarding flow for the enterprise tier has been nothing short of stellar-

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: you took the initial prototype we sketched in early May, iterated on the feedback loops with the sales team, and delivered a production-ready version by July 12th, all while juggling the unexpected VPC rollout. The reduction in onboarding time from an average of 14 days down to 6 days is already showing up in our early-stage churn metrics.

turns.speaker: Rachel Goldstein
turns.text: Thanks, Nadia. It was a team effort-big thanks to Maya in UX and Tom on the backend for pulling the API hooks together on such short notice.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Absolutely, and I’ll make sure they get the kudos in the next all-hands. The second person I want to highlight is Daniel.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Your rewrite of the query engine not only unlocked multi-tenant indexing but also laid the groundwork for the VPC namespace support we just announced. The performance benchmarks you posted last week-average query latency dropping from 420 ms to 180 ms on our largest tenant-are a game changer for our enterprise customers.

turns.speaker: Daniel Okonkwo
turns.text: Appreciate it, Nadia. It was a massive effort across the team, especially pulling in the data-science folks to validate the new caching strategy.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: And let’s not forget the extra hours you and the contractors put in to get the Terraform modules production-ready before the August 21st beta launch. That automation pipeline now handles 20 VPCs a week, which means we can scale the enterprise tier without hitting a bottleneck.

turns.speaker: James Mbeki
turns.text: From a finance perspective, those engineering wins translate directly into better gross margins-our model shows we’ll stay near that 71% target even as we add the $15 K per-seat VPC cost into the enterprise pricing.

turns.speaker: Alex Rivera
turns.text: I also want to add that the faster onboarding you mentioned, Rachel, is already reflected in our pipeline velocity. Our average deal cycle for enterprise prospects has shrunk from 90 days to about 68 days, which is huge for Q4 forecasting.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Exactly, Alex. And that’s why we’re so optimistic about hitting the $8.4 M ARR target by year-end-especially with the two $1.2 M deals we just discussed and the pipeline you’re managing.

turns.speaker: Sarah Chen
turns.text: Kudos to the whole solutions team as well-those demo VPCs we can spin up in five minutes have been a real differentiator in the last few demos.

turns.speaker: Nadia Hassan
turns.text: Thanks, Sarah. Okay, so to recap: Rachel, Daniel-big thanks for the product breakthroughs; the rest of the team for keeping the ship steady during that four-hour outage in August. Let’s keep that momentum into Q4, stay focused on the three priorities we outlined-scaling the VPC automation, finalizing the health-data compliance roadmap, and tightening our net-revenue-retention initiatives. If anyone needs anything, my virtual door is always open. Thanks, everyone!
